title: Pope Leo XIV Draws 600,000 to Paris's Champs-Élysées for Historic Mass
summary:
More than 600,000 people registered to attend Pope Leo XIV's outdoor mass in Paris on Saturday, packing the Champs-Élysées and the Place de la Concorde. The American pope greeted the crowds from his popemobile during a two-kilometre parade along the famous avenue, which was closed to traffic for the event. The turnout was a striking sign of the Catholic Church's enduring appeal in France, a country that is officially secular (meaning the government and religion are kept separate) but has deep Catholic roots.

The choice of Place de la Concorde was symbolic — and controversial. Organizers said it was the only central Paris location big enough for the expected crowds. But critics who strongly support France's secular laws argued that the square represents the Republic itself and that another site, like the Invalides, would have been more appropriate. Pope Benedict XVI celebrated mass there in 2008 for 240,000 people.

Despite the debate, the atmosphere was festive. People of many faiths — and no faith — came to see the pope. "The message of Pope Leo goes well beyond Catholic people; he speaks about social justice," said Leontine Joseph, 42, who attended with two friends of Moroccan origin. Thierry Chen, 40, a Parisian entrepreneur who is not Catholic, said, "People are seeing a lot of really terrible images. This kind of event reminds people of what is really important in life."

Pope Leo's four-day visit began Friday at the newly restored Notre-Dame Cathedral, the first papal visit there since the 2019 fire. He also spoke at the Catholic Institute of Paris, where he said he was surprised by the rise in adult baptisms — which have tripled since 2016 to 13,000 this year. Still, experts note that overall baptisms have dropped sharply, from 513,000 in 1980 to 186,000 in 2024. The pope urged French Catholics to keep their faith alive "even amid the thorns" of a secular world.
why_it_matters: The event shows how a country can be officially secular yet still shaped by religious tradition — and it raises real questions for young Europeans about how a diverse, multi-faith society decides what belongs in its most symbolic public spaces.

background_read: France's version of secularism is called laïcité, and it grew out of laws passed in the early 1900s that formally separated church and state. Under laïcité, the government stays out of religion and religion is expected to stay out of government business — which is why some critics objected to a religious mass on the Place de la Concorde, a central square tied to the Republic and to the French Revolution.
The Champs-Élysées is Paris's most famous avenue, running from the Arc de Triomphe down to the Place de la Concorde, and it is regularly closed for national celebrations and parades.

Pope Leo XIV is the American pope leading the Catholic Church. His four-day trip began at Notre-Dame Cathedral, the medieval Paris church that was devastated by a fire in 2019 and has since been restored and reopened.
Two popes had been there before him: Pope Benedict XVI celebrated mass at the Invalides in 2008 for 240,000 people, the figure the article uses to compare turnout.

The turnout is striking because French Catholic practice has shrunk for decades. The article notes that adult baptisms have risen even as total baptisms fell from 513,000 in 1980 to 186,000 in 2024 — a reminder that a huge public event and long-term decline can be true at the same time.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: a sign of living faith
perspectives.description: Organizers and pilgrims point to the enormous turnout, the festive mood and the rising number of adult baptisms as proof the Church still speaks to people. Even non-Catholics like Thierry Chen said the event reminded Parisians of what matters.

perspectives.perspective: Critical: it crossed a line of French secularism
perspectives.description: Defenders of strict laïcité argued that the Place de la Concorde stands for the Republic itself and should not host a religious ceremony, suggesting the Invalides instead. For them, keeping religion out of state symbols is not hostility to faith but the guarantee of equal treatment for everyone.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral/analytical: a symbolic event against a long decline
perspectives.description: The numbers cut both ways. A crowd of 600,000 in the streets sits alongside total baptisms falling from 513,000 in 1980 to 186,000 in 2024, showing that big public moments and shrinking weekly practice can coexist in modern France.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: what this means for the Church in Europe
perspectives.description: The pope's closing appeal to keep faith alive 'even amid the thorns' of a secular world frames the next chapter: whether rising adult baptisms and historic venues like a restored Notre-Dame can renew Catholic life, or whether such mass gatherings become impressive but occasional exceptions.
